narrative:
The model predicted a 63% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), while students who were accepted averaged around the middle of their class (5.8). Your first-year ranking also mattered, though less so; being in the third decile rather than the sixth-decile average of accepted students added further concern. Your LSAT score of 22 was the second-most important factor and pulled the prediction even more toward failure; accepted students averaged 37.

These three pieces of information—your recent class standing, your LSAT performance, and your earlier class standing—together outweighed other details such as your undergraduate GPA, family income bracket, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time. None of those played a meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT. Stronger grades in your remaining studies and a significantly higher LSAT score would directly address the factors that led to this rejection. Consider working with an advisor to build a clear plan for both.
